title: Accessibility Auditing
subtopics: Manual evaluation of real interaction flows
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of accessibility auditing.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on accessibility auditing and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Accessibility Auditing matters because interface appearance should reflect actual state while remaining understandable to keyboard, touch and assistive-technology users.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Browser accessibility inspectors; Automated accessibility checks; Keyboard testing; Contrast testing; Manual evaluation of real interaction flows. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to understand
items: Manual evaluation of real interaction flows

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Accessibility Auditing
content_blocks.code:
<button class="rounded-lg bg-blue-700 px-4 py-2 text-white focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-700 motion-reduce:transition-none">
  Save changes
</button>
content_blocks.expected_output: The control has a visible keyboard focus indicator and suppresses nonessential transitions for reduced-motion users.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to accessibility auditing, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Complete the linked practical exercise “Accessibility audit”. Run an accessibility audit covering keyboard focus, contrast, labels and narrow-screen behavior.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to accessibility auditing.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to accessibility auditing.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: The control has a visible keyboard focus indicator and suppresses nonessential transitions for reduced-motion users.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying accessibility auditing without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Accessibility Auditing is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
